name: Kubernetes
tagline: Schedules containers, heals them and routes traffic to them.

howItWorks.title: What it is and where it sits
howItWorks.body:
Kubernetes keeps declared state true: you describe pods, it converges the cluster toward them.
Pod networking is L3, Services balance at L4, Ingress and Gateway API route at L7.
Every pod gets its own IP; a CNI plugin wires pods across nodes.
One cluster is a failure domain; plan several for blast-radius isolation.
Side note: OKD and OpenShift add Routes, SCCs and an installer on this same core.

howItWorks.title: Components and architecture
howItWorks.body:
The API server is the only front door to cluster state.
etcd stores desired state; only the API server talks to it.
The scheduler binds pods to nodes; controller loops reconcile actual to desired.
The kubelet runs pods through the container runtime; kube-proxy programs Service rules.
CoreDNS answers service names; the CNI plugin provides pod networking and NetworkPolicy.

howItWorks.title: Request and data flow
howItWorks.body:
kubectl sends a manifest; the API server authenticates, authorizes, validates and persists it.
The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet, which creates pods.
The scheduler picks a node; the kubelet pulls the image and starts containers.
Passing readiness adds the pod to Service endpoints (EndpointSlices).
Inbound traffic hits a node; kube-proxy rewrites the destination to a ready pod IP.

howItWorks.title: Services and Ingress (L4 and L7)
howItWorks.body:
ClusterIP gives pods one stable virtual IP and DNS name inside the cluster.
NodePort opens a port in 30000-32767 on every node, forwarding to the Service.
LoadBalancer asks a cloud controller, or MetalLB on bare metal, for an external address.
An Ingress or Gateway API controller terminates TLS and routes by Host and path.
Readiness gates endpoints: unready pods leave rotation without restarts.

howItWorks.title: High availability and scaling
howItWorks.body:
Run three or five control-plane nodes with etcd quorum; spread workers across zones.
HPA reads metrics-server and sets replicas between min and max.
Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter adds nodes when pods stay Pending.
PodDisruptionBudgets and topology spread constraints keep replicas alive through drains and zone loss.
Deployments roll out with maxSurge and maxUnavailable; rollout undo reverts.

howItWorks.title: Security
howItWorks.body:
RBAC: Role and RoleBinding grant verbs on resources; verify with kubectl auth can-i.
Pods accept all traffic until a NetworkPolicy selects them; start default-deny, then allow.
NetworkPolicy needs a CNI that enforces it, such as Calico or Cilium.
Pod Security Admission enforces baseline or restricted profiles per namespace.
Use short-lived ServiceAccount tokens, private registries and image scanning.

howItWorks.title: Observability and troubleshooting
howItWorks.body:
Start at kubectl get, describe and events; most failures name themselves there.
Pending: no capacity or unmet scheduling rule. ImagePullBackOff: wrong image or credentials.
CrashLoopBackOff: read kubectl logs --previous; OOMKilled means the memory limit was hit.
Empty endpoints mean a selector mismatch or a failing readiness probe.
Scrape kube-state-metrics and node metrics; alert on restarts, Pending pods and node pressure.

howItWorks.title: What sits in front
howItWorks.body:
Users reach the cluster through the Edge: a load balancer, an Ingress controller or a Gateway API implementation.
NodePort opens a fixed port on every node; a LoadBalancer Service asks a cloud controller or MetalLB for an address.
An Ingress or Gateway controller terminates TLS and routes by Host and path to Services.
On the Platform, kube-proxy rules then pick a ready pod.

howItWorks.title: What sits behind
howItWorks.body:
A Service selects pods by label; EndpointSlices list the ready ones.
Pods run through the container runtime, for example containerd or CRI-O, pulling images from a registry.
Pods reach databases, queues and caches over ordinary Service DNS names.
Persistent volumes attach through CSI drivers to Infrastructure storage.

howItWorks.title: Alternatives
howItWorks.body:
Nomad: simpler scheduler for mixed container and non-container workloads.
Docker Swarm or plain Compose: a few hosts, no cluster machinery.
Managed services such as EKS, GKE or AKS: someone else runs the control plane.
OpenShift or OKD: Kubernetes plus a built-in router, installer and stricter defaults.

flow: kubectl applies a manifest to the API server.
The API server authenticates, authorizes via RBAC and persists to etcd.
The Deployment controller creates a ReplicaSet and pods.
The scheduler binds each pod to a node.
The kubelet pulls the image and starts containers.
A readiness probe passes; the pod joins the Service endpoints.
An external proxy or Ingress sends the request to a node port or Service.
kube-proxy forwards it to a pod; NetworkPolicy permits the hop.
HPA adds replicas when CPU crosses the target.

deploy.summary: A two-node kind lab: Ingress, NodePort, NetworkPolicy, HPA, RBAC and rollouts.
prerequisites: Linux host with Docker, 4 GB free RAM
Ports 8080 and 8443 free on the host
Placeholders in <angle brackets> are yours to set

steps.title: Create the cluster
steps.code:
cat > kind-lab.yaml <<'EOF'
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
name: lab
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
    image: kindest/node:v1.31.0
    kubeadmConfigPatches:
      - |
        kind: InitConfiguration
        nodeRegistration:
          kubeletExtraArgs:
            node-labels: "ingress-ready=true"
    extraPortMappings:
      - {containerPort: 80, hostPort: 8080, protocol: TCP}
      - {containerPort: 443, hostPort: 8443, protocol: TCP}
  - role: worker
    image: kindest/node:v1.31.0
EOF
kind create cluster --config kind-lab.yaml
kubectl get nodes -o wide
steps.note: Both nodes reach Ready in about two minutes. Match the node image to your kind release notes.

steps.title: Install the ingress controller (L7)
steps.code:
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/controller-v1.11.2/deploy/static/provider/kind/deploy.yaml
kubectl -n ingress-nginx wait --for=condition=ready pod \
  --selector=app.kubernetes.io/component=controller --timeout=180s
steps.note: This is the kind-specific manifest. It relies on the ingress-ready label set above. The ingress-nginx project was announced as retired in 2026, so treat it as a lab-only example; Gateway API controllers such as Traefik, Envoy Gateway or Istio are the current choices.

steps.title: Deploy an app: Service (L4) and Ingress (L7)
steps.code:
kubectl create namespace dev
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl -n dev apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: web}
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: web}}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27.3
          ports: [{containerPort: 80}]
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi}
            limits: {memory: 128Mi}
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /, port: 80}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: web}
spec:
  selector: {app: web}
  ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 80}]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: web}
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
    - host: web.localtest.me
      http:
        paths:
          - {path: /, pathType: Prefix, backend: {service: {name: web, port: {number: 80}}}}
EOF
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://web.localtest.me:8080/
steps.note: The Service defaults to ClusterIP; set spec.type to NodePort to change that. localtest.me resolves to 127.0.0.1.

steps.title: NodePort: expose the Service on every node
steps.code:
kubectl -n dev expose deploy web --name web-np --type NodePort --port 80
kubectl -n dev patch svc web-np -p '{"spec":{"ports":[{"port":80,"nodePort":30080}]}}'
NODE_IP=$(docker inspect -f '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}' lab-worker)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://$NODE_IP:30080/
kubectl -n dev get svc web-np -o wide
steps.note: Real nodes need 30000-32767 open; point a proxy at <NODE_IP>:30080.

steps.title: NetworkPolicy: default deny, then allow ingress
steps.code:
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl -n dev apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: default-deny}
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-ingress-controller}
spec:
  podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx}
EOF
kubectl -n dev run probe --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://web
steps.note: The probe must time out. If it succeeds, your CNI does not enforce NetworkPolicy; install Calico or Cilium.

steps.title: HPA with metrics-server
steps.code:
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/download/v0.7.2/components.yaml
kubectl -n kube-system patch deploy metrics-server --type=json \
  -p '[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]'
kubectl -n dev autoscale deploy web --cpu-percent=70 --min=2 --max=6
kubectl -n dev get hpa
steps.note: Needs CPU requests on the pods. The insecure-tls flag is for kind only.

steps.title: RBAC: a deployer in dev
steps.code:
kubectl -n dev create role deployer --verb=get,list,watch,create,update,patch --resource=deployments,pods
kubectl -n dev create rolebinding deployer-jane --role=deployer --user=jane
kubectl -n dev auth can-i create deployments --as=jane
kubectl -n qa auth can-i create deployments --as=jane
steps.note: The first answer is yes, the second is no. Roles are namespaced; use ClusterRole for cluster scope.

steps.title: Roll out and roll back
steps.code:
kubectl -n dev set image deploy/web web=nginx:1.27.4
kubectl -n dev rollout status deploy/web
kubectl -n dev rollout history deploy/web
kubectl -n dev rollout undo deploy/web
steps.note: Undo returns to the previous ReplicaSet. Use rollout pause to hold a rollout halfway.

verify: Endpoints populated: kubectl -n dev get endpoints web
HPA reads metrics: kubectl -n dev get hpa
pitfalls: No resource requests means HPA shows unknown and the scheduler packs blindly.
NetworkPolicy does nothing without an enforcing CNI.
A failing readiness probe keeps the Service endpoints empty.
Default-deny also blocks DNS; allow egress to kube-dns.
NodePort range is 30000-32767; firewalls and the external LB must allow it.
Memory limit hit means OOMKilled; check with kubectl describe pod.
A Service with no ready pods has empty endpoints; check selectors first.
keyPoints: Control plane decides; kubelets on nodes execute.
Services balance at L4; Ingress and Gateway route at L7.
NodePort, LoadBalancer or Ingress connect outside traffic to pods.
NetworkPolicy and RBAC isolate; HPA and rollouts scale and ship safely.
quickDeploy: Create a kind cluster with two nodes.
Install an ingress controller and expose an app.
Add a NodePort Service and test it.
Lock down with NetworkPolicy, then autoscale.
osiNote: Services balance at L4; Ingress and Gateway route at L7.
production: Run three control-plane nodes; back up etcd on a schedule.
Set requests and limits on every pod; enforce ResourceQuota.
Default-deny NetworkPolicy; least-privilege RBAC per namespace.
Use readiness probes, PodDisruptionBudgets and rollout undo.
Alert on pod restarts, pending pods and node pressure.
